segments.text: Aromatic compounds, typified by benzene, behave very differently from the alkenes their structure superficially resembles — they resist addition reactions that would destroy their unusually stable ring system, and instead undergo substitution that preserves it.

Benzene (C₆H₆) is a planar, hexagonal ring where each carbon is sp² hybridised, and the six unhybridized p orbitals overlap continuously around the ring, delocalising six π electrons over the whole structure rather than confining them to three separate double bonds. This delocalisation provides substantial extra stability (
resonance/aromatic stabilisation energy
) beyond what three isolated double bonds would have — explaining why benzene resists the addition reactions typical of ordinary alkenes.
Aromaticity

in general requires a molecule to be cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and to contain 4n+2 π electrons (Hückel’s rule) — a specific electron count that produces extra stability in a way exactly analogous to the closed-shell stability of noble gas electron configurations (Chapter 1).
Because the aromatic ring is electron-rich (delocalised π system) but reacting via addition would destroy its stabilisation, aromatic compounds instead react with electrophiles via
substitution

, restoring aromaticity in the final product. The mechanism proceeds through a positively charged, non-aromatic intermediate (the arenium ion), which then loses a proton to regenerate the stable aromatic ring — common examples include nitration, sulfonation, halogenation, and Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation.
An existing substituent on the ring influences both the rate and the position (
ortho/para
or
meta
) of further substitution.
Ortho/para-directing

groups (like –OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃, or alkyl groups) donate electron density into the ring (by resonance or induction), stabilising the intermediate cation most effectively when the new substituent adds ortho or para to them.
Meta-directing
groups (like –NO₂, –CN, –COOH) withdraw electron density, and the ring positions least destabilised by this withdrawal turn out to be the meta positions.
Groups that donate electron density into the ring are
activating
(they speed up EAS reactions, since they make the ring more nucleophilic) and are typically also ortho/para-directors. Groups that withdraw electron density are
deactivating

(they slow EAS reactions) and are typically meta-directors, with one notable exception: halogens are deactivating (due to strong inductive electron withdrawal) yet still ortho/para-directing (due to resonance donation of a lone pair into the ring) — a useful example of how inductive and resonance effects can act in opposite directions.

Beyond direct ring substitution, aromatic chemistry includes reactions of substituents attached to the ring (such as oxidation of an alkyl side chain to a carboxylic acid, or reduction of a nitro group to an amine) — transformations that combine the ring’s directing effects with the functional-group chemistry developed in Chapter 14, and are frequently used together in multi-step aromatic synthesis problems.

items.text: Aromaticity (cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, 4n+2 π electrons per Hückel’s rule) confers substantial extra stability, explaining benzene’s preference for substitution over addition.
Electrophilic aromatic substitution proceeds through a cationic arenium ion intermediate, restoring aromaticity upon proton loss.
Existing substituents direct further substitution to ortho/para or meta positions based on whether they donate (ortho/para) or withdraw (meta) electron density from the ring.

Activating groups are generally ortho/para-directors and deactivating groups meta-directors, except halogens, which are deactivating but ortho/para-directing due to competing inductive and resonance effects.
